column3: Its account of unjustly killing prophets adds a broad condemnation of wrongful killing, but not this episode's accusation of tyranny.
A group claiming collective victory supplies a limited parallel to the contested factional support behind Musa's intervention.
Contrasts God's will to accept repentance with desire-led pressure toward collective deviation.
The prior day's renewed plea for help establishes the immediate factional pressure that precedes the attempted strike.
It supplies the earlier killing while answering a partisan cry for help, the event invoked in the accusation.
Directly joins striking with being tyrannical, closely clarifying the charge made against Musa.
Musa later acknowledges the killing and fears retaliation, confirming the lasting liability raised here.
Musa vows not to use his strength as support for criminals, setting a clear boundary for the help sought in the focus.
Its warning of a severe seizure supplies a consequential contrast to force used without repair.
It gives the strongest general measure for the gravity of killing a person without right and its opposite, preserving life.
The reward of believers' good works does not clarify the conflict, killing, or charge of tyranny here.
The passive claim that something is intended offers only a distant parallel to contested motives.
Deceptive speech recasts a prohibited act as a desirable intention, a limited parallel to how Musa's act is read.
Musa's confession of self-wronging and forgiveness immediately frames the earlier killing as a matter requiring repair.
It portrays a people immobilized by those they call tyrants, adding the social fear associated with that label.
Divine creative authority does not add to the focus's human conflict over killing and reform.
Even mutually supporting beings cannot meet the Qur'an's challenge, offering a limited counterpoint to factional backing.
The divine name al-Jabbar distinguishes God's authority from the human accusation of acting as a tyrant.
It recalls Musa's killing, rescue, and later preparation, placing the incident within his larger accountable history.
The warning that leaders plan to kill Musa shows the immediate danger into which this confrontation develops.
Those proposing murder promise themselves later righteousness, exposing the hollow claim that harm can precede reform.
The later divine call of Musa adds no direct understanding of the disputed intervention.
This family dispute over resurrection does not illuminate the focus's force, killing, or repair themes.
The fall of peoples stronger in force offers only a broad warning about reliance on coercive power.
Goodness to parents is explicitly opposed to being a disobedient tyrant, sharpening the moral contrast in the charge.
Musa's fearful departure and plea for rescue are the direct outcome of the danger announced after this scene.
It makes repair an indispensable companion to repentance, defining what a genuine turn from wrongdoing requires.
The bare call to Musa does not add to the present accusation or its consequences.
Its reference to Abraham as of a following party offers only a remote lexical parallel to communal allegiance.
It gives the eventual failure of every stubborn tyrant, reinforcing the seriousness of the accusation's moral category.
It repeats the anti-tyrant contrast already supplied more directly by 19:14 without adding to the focus.
Musa's request for guidance on the road extends the focus's fear into a route away from violent entanglement.
The severity of the Lord's seizure distinguishes divine judgment from a person's contested use of force.
This correction of Noah's familial claim does not clarify killing, tyranny, or reform in the focus.
Abraham's sound heart offers no specific link to the focus's immediate conflict.
It links faith to righteous action, truth, and patience, supplying a positive social frame against coercive wrongdoing.
Its demand for the reason an innocent girl was killed intensifies the focus's concern with lethal wrongdoing.
Rejected oaths to follow a warner do not materially explain the focus's accusation.
It presents repentance joined to righteous action as a real return to God, closely supporting the focus's reform criterion.
It contrasts an unspecified intended harm with the Lord's intended right guidance, only broadly relevant to intention.
By returning good and evil acts to the doer, it frames harmful force and repair as accountable personal action.
The inadequacy of false gods against harm does not illuminate the dispute between Musa and the man.
The question to Iblis about refusing prostration does not add to the focus.
The condemned wish to return and do other than their former deeds gives a late, failed contrast to timely reform.
The response to believers with righteous deeds does not specifically address coercion or repair.
It explicitly calls those who hold to revelation and establish prayer reformers, supplying a positive content for muslihin.
Signs in horizons and selves do not clarify the focus's conflict over motive and force.
Divine guidance of whom God wills is only a broad parallel to the verse's repeated language of intending.
An accusation that someone intended evil and a proposed penalty parallels the public reading of disputed conduct.
Human presumption after mercy does not add to the focus's killing and tyranny accusation.
Salih's call to reverence offers only a remote positive association with reform.
The Lord's merciful intention toward vulnerable orphans contrasts broadly with intention perceived as harmful.
Universal glorification does not clarify human force, killing, or reform here.
It explicitly defines corrupters as those who do not reform in the land, directly sharpening the focus's final contrast.
It contrasts seeking God's face with pursuing worldly ornament, offering a limited lens for competing intentions.
It depicts authority answering faith and righteous action with a good reward and gentle command rather than tyranny.
Deception exposes an enemy and harmful consequences, but it only indirectly parallels the focus's hostile confrontation.
The enduring reward for righteous deeds gives only general positive background for reform.
The request for idols after deliverance does not add to the focus's disputed intervention.
It joins arrogant tyranny to arguing without authority, clarifying a pattern of domineering conduct.
The affirmation of God's oneness and dominance does not address the human accusation in the focus.
God's effective accomplishment of what He wills is too general to resolve the human intentions under dispute.
Its later reference to yesterday and changed fortune offers only a distant echo of the focus's recalled prior day.
The list of righteous prophets does not add to the focus's force or reform question.
It makes even accidental killing subject to defined compensatory repair, strongly framing the liability raised in the focus.
God's guardianship of the righteous does not specify the contested use of force.
The transience of worldly growth does not clarify killing, tyranny, or reform in this scene.
Their intended plotting and its reversal offer a limited parallel to harmful intent meeting consequence.
Its procedures for just documentation and testimony give a distant institutional model for preventing wrong and dispute.
Its broad faith-and-righteous-action criterion does not specifically explain the focus's accusation.
Musa later gives practical aid without force and turns humbly to God, offering a meaningful contrast to the disputed intervention.
Admission among the righteous through faith and works adds no specific insight beyond earlier repair parallels.
Abraham's withdrawal from an enemy of God does not illuminate the focus's use of force.
Companionship with the righteous does not clarify the focus's charge of tyranny or failed reform.
Kindness to parents is not materially connected to this conflict.
The gardens promised for faith and righteous deeds do not add to the focus's immediate moral dispute.
The test posed by the number of guardians of Hell does not clarify the focus.
It identifies a person's wish to continue wrongdoing ahead, a limited parallel to intention bent away from reform.
The reminder of human creation does not add to the focus's killing or coercion themes.
Repentance, repair, holding fast to God, and sincerity provide a concrete multi-part alternative to corrupt conduct.
A family pledge of safe return does not materially explain the focus's confrontation.
The final reward for believers' righteous works adds no specific insight beyond earlier cards.
It counts hardship and action against an enemy as righteous work, but does not distinguish force from tyranny here.
It models action purified from wanting human repayment or thanks, only broadly relevant to the focus's contested intention.
The proud group's bare rejection does not clarify the focus.
It addresses suspected deceit while grounding support in God and believers, usefully qualifying how danger and backing are assessed.
It ties each self to what it earns and seeks pardon for error, reinforcing accountable action without overburdening.
It combines repentance, faith, and righteous action as the path out of corruption, though it repeats earlier repair evidence.
Its call to advance good for one's own selves offers only a broad personal-action counterpart to reform.
A stated refusal to burden Musa and a claim to righteousness provide a limited local contrast in human intention.
Musa's later demand to investigate the women's plotting shows care for truth before release, only distantly related to the focus.
It rewards devout obedience and righteous action but does not specifically address coercion or repair.
Creation and gardens as signs of God do not clarify the focus's accusation.
It explicitly denies that the messenger is a compeller and assigns him remembrance, directly contrasting tyranny with proper guidance.
Musa acknowledges that he committed the earlier act while astray, directly deepening the self-critical frame of the focus.
Divine guidance and repair of their condition supplies a positive meaning of islah, though outside this conflict.
Noah's plea to remove disbelievers offers only a difficult contrast between destructive prayer and the focus's charge of tyranny.
It explicitly says God does not set right the work of corrupters, directly defining the boundary invoked by not being reformers.
The bare designation of the companions of the right adds no relevant detail.
Turning from one who desires only worldly life supplies a focused warning about intention narrowed away from higher guidance.
Pharaoh's division, oppression, and killing of sons supplies the clearest local model of tyranny in the land.
The father's declaration that Musa escaped the wrongdoing people directly completes the danger set in motion by the focus.
The description of strength joined to trustworthiness supplies a constructive standard against force that is read as tyranny.
Musa's stipulation that there be no aggression against him gives a local contractual contrast to coercive conduct.
It expressly commands doing good and forbids seeking corruption in the land, directly clarifying the focus's reform-versus-tyranny contrast.
It denies the final good outcome to those who seek exaltation or corruption in the land, closely matching the charge against Musa.
Pharaoh directly confronts Musa with the earlier killing, forming the closest parallel accusation elsewhere in the Moses narrative.
Pharaoh turns that past act into an accusation of ingratitude and disbelief, showing how a killing can be rhetorically weaponized.
Musa's flight in fear and later divine wisdom link the killing to accountability, escape, and mission.
Musa names Pharaoh's enslavement of the Children of Israel, exposing the coercive rule behind Pharaoh's accusation.
The command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed directly supplies the narrative's authoritative diagnosis of tyranny.
Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh because he has exceeded bounds, extending the focus's concern with force into its wider conflict.
The command to speak gently to Pharaoh contrasts prophetic correction with the coercion associated with a tyrant.
Moses and Aaron fear Pharaoh's haste and transgression, giving a parallel scene of anticipated abusive force.
Pharaoh's threat of mutilation and crucifixion is an explicit instance of power becoming terror and domination.
Pharaoh's chiefs propose killing the believers' sons and sparing their women, directly portraying oppressive political violence.
It calls Pharaoh exalted in the land and among the corrupters, a close narrative counterpart to the focus's language.
It forbids killing the soul God has made sacred except by right, directly grounding the focus's recalled killing in a general norm.
The warning about intentional killing of a believer supplies the Quran's most severe liability frame for deliberate homicide.
It forbids taking life except by right, supplying a direct moral boundary for the contested attempted violence.
It names unlawful killing among the gravest violations, reinforcing the focus's contrast between killing and reform.
It prohibits cooperation in sin and transgression, directly qualifying when answering another's cry for help becomes wrongful support.
It commands justice even toward a hated people, directly challenging force driven by factional hostility.
Its treatment of violent corruption in the land clarifies the public stakes of force that destroys social order.
Racing into sin, transgression, and consuming the unlawful supplies a broad pattern of organized wrongdoing.
The plea of oppressed men, women, and children distinguishes legitimate rescue from partisan backing that perpetuates harm.
Intercession for good or evil makes each act of support carry a share of its moral consequence.
It requires justice even against oneself, parents, or relatives, directly countering loyalty-driven partiality.
Those who claim to be reformers while causing corruption closely parallel the focus's dispute over whether force is reform or tyranny.
It permits fighting those who fight while prohibiting transgression, giving a decisive limit on responsive force.
It depicts a person who spreads corruption and destroys life and livelihood while presenting himself otherwise, closely fitting false reform claims.
It explicitly distinguishes the corrupter from the reformer, naming the central evaluative boundary in the focus.
It forbids corruption in the land after its reform, directly pairing the two terms that conclude the focus.
Shuayb's prohibition on diminishing others' due and spreading corruption supplies a concrete social content for reform.
Shuayb states that he desires only reform to the extent he can, furnishing the clearest positive formulation of intending islah.
God does not destroy towns while their people are reformers, giving reform a communal significance opposed to wrongdoing.
Justice in measure and refusal to spread corruption give an economic application of the focus's repair standard.
Breaking covenant and spreading corruption in the land shows another form of social damage opposed to reform.
The command of justice and excellence, and prohibition of transgression, establishes a general ethical alternative to tyrannical force.
It limits retaliation to the measure of the harm received, directly constraining the escalation of force.
Permission to fight is tied to having been wronged, distinguishing defensive force from domination.
The nine men who corrupt in the land and do not reform closely repeat the focus's explicit opposition.
Their plot to kill Salih and his family exposes collective violence concealed through a false public denial.
Corruption appearing on land and sea through human hands frames harm as consequential rather than reformative.
It permits proportionate response but elevates pardon and reform, directly setting repair above retaliation.
It recognizes defense after oppression, clarifying that not every use of force is tyrannical.
It condemns those who wrong people and tyrannize in the land without right, nearly stating the focus's charge in general form.
It requires force against a transgressing party only until it returns to God's command, then justice and reconciliation.
The command to reconcile believers supplies a direct positive social alternative to factional escalation.
It requires kindness and justice toward those who do not fight believers, limiting hostility by conduct rather than identity.
It commands acceptance of peace when the opposing party inclines to it, countering unnecessary continuation of conflict.
Mutual support among believers is defined by enjoining right and forbidding wrong, not unconditional partisan assistance.
It forbids obedience to extravagant leaders who cause corruption and do not reform, extending the focus's tyranny criterion to leadership.
It joins refusal to defraud people with refusal to spread corruption, adding concrete conduct to the meaning of reform.
Pharaoh's proposal to kill Musa shows tyrannical power treating religious dissent as a threat to be eliminated.
The believing man challenges Pharaoh's plan to kill Musa merely for declaring his Lord, directly exposing unjust political violence.
Repelling evil with what is better gives a practical non-escalatory response to hostility.
It characterizes earlier peoples as those who transgressed in the lands, supplying a broad historical pattern of tyrannical excess.
Their multiplication of corruption in the lands reinforces the link between transgression and social ruin.
